title: Metrics monitoring platform (collect, aggregate, graph, alert)
statement:
We have a big deployment with hundreds of machines each of which is exposing thousands of statistics. You can think that each statistic is represented by the tuple [source, metric-name, value].
We want to be able to collect and aggregate those tuples in a scalable manner. The main consumers for this system are:

A graphing system - For a certain metric-name, plot a set of sources from time t1 to t2
e.g. Memory usage of host-1, host-2, host-3 for the past week
An alerting system- Issue an alert (email, etc) when a certain metric-name goes above/below a certain threshold
e.g. Memory usage goes above 70%

variants.text: Design a metrics platform: services publish metrics; store, aggregate, and display on a dashboard; implement alerting thresholds.

Hundreds of machines, each exposing thousands of statistics as [source, metric-name, value]. Collect and aggregate them; consumers are a graphing system (plot sources t1→t2) and an alerting system (above/below a threshold).
Design metric monitoring system.
variants.note: Self verdict: strong hire — explained everything, and even discussed out-of-scope things.

variants.text: Metrics aggregator, monitoring system — metrics aggregating, querying, graphing and alarming.
Metrics aggregation and visualization.
variants.note: Was driving the interview most of the time.

variants.text: Host health across three data centres, hundreds of thousands of hosts, with history and a UI (merged here — same system).
Metrics gathering and aggregation — Blind ×2, Glassdoor (lesson 2.3).

LinkedIn runs hundreds of thousands of hosts across three data centres. Design a system that tracks each host's health now and over time, with a UI engineers use for troubleshooting — start with the overall picture, then go deep on parts.

guide.gist: The most reported LinkedIn design question. Collect `[source, metric, value]` from hundreds of machines, store it as **time series**, let people **graph** any metric for any hosts over time, and **alert** on thresholds. The hard parts: very high **write volume**, fast **range queries**, and alerting that does not miss or spam.
clarify: How many sources and metrics, how often?
Decides write rate — the main number in this question.
How long to keep data, and at what detail?
Raw for days, then downsampled (1-min, 1-hour) — decides storage.
How fresh must graphs and alerts be?
Alerts within ~1 minute usually; graphs a few seconds behind is fine.
Which queries? One metric for a few hosts (t1→t2), or aggregates (p99 across a cluster)?
Decides the data layout and pre-aggregation.
Push or pull — can we put an agent on every machine?
Decides the collection path.
numbers: 500 machines × 2,000 stats × every 10 s = 100K points/s (scale ×100 for LinkedIn-size: 10M/s).
A point ≈ 16 bytes compressed (Gorilla-style delta encoding gets ~1.4 bytes) → small per point, large in total.
Graph query: 3 hosts × 1 week × 1 point/min ≈ 30K points — cheap if data is stored by (metric, source, time).
parts: Collects stats, batches every 10 s, compresses, sends. Buffers on local disk if the collector is unreachable.
Receive batches and write to Kafka (durable buffer, absorbs spikes, lets several consumers read).
Stores points keyed by (metric, source) and time, compressed in time blocks. Sharded by series.
Build 1-min and 1-hour averages/max; delete raw data after N days.
Picks the right resolution for the time range (a week → 1-min rollups, not raw).
Evaluates rules on the stream (or on recent data every 30 s); dedupes and routes to email/pager.
deep: Data layout
Group points by series (metric + source) and time block (e.g. 2 hours). A graph query reads a few contiguous blocks. Compress timestamps and values with deltas — this is why TSDBs are so small.
Downsampling
Nobody needs 10-second points from last year. Keep raw for ~2 weeks, 1-minute for months, 1-hour for years. The query service chooses the resolution from the range.
Alerting that works
"Above 70% for 5 minutes", not "above 70% once" (avoids flapping). Treat **missing data as a signal** — a dead host sends nothing. Group and dedupe alerts during incidents.
Cardinality
The real danger: a label like user_id creates millions of series and kills the TSDB. Limit labels, and reject or sample high-cardinality metrics.
followups: Write rate goes 10× — what breaks first?
The TSDB write path. Add shards by series, batch harder on agents, drop or sample low-value metrics. Kafka absorbs short spikes.
Graph a cluster-wide p99 over 30 days fast.
Pre-aggregate per cluster in rollups (or store histograms/sketches); never compute it from raw points at query time.
The monitoring system itself goes down.
Run it per data centre; each DC monitors itself and the others. Agents buffer locally. A separate tiny heartbeat checker watches the monitor.
Host health across 3 data centres (the InterviewDB version).
Per-DC collectors and storage, a global view that merges them, and a current-state store (latest status per host) for "what is unhealthy now".
How do you avoid alert spam?
For-duration conditions, grouping by service, dedupe, severity levels, silence windows during maintenance.
mistakes: Writing every point straight into a SQL table.
No downsampling — storage grows forever, week-long graphs are slow.
Alerting on a single sample (flapping).
Forgetting that a silent host is a failure.
Ignoring cardinality.
guide.say: "Agents batch to Kafka, a sharded time-series store keeps compressed series with rollups, queries pick the resolution from the range, and alerts evaluate for-duration rules on the stream — with missing data treated as an alert."

fr: Machines send [source, metric, value] every few seconds
Graph one metric for chosen hosts from t1 to t2
Alert rules: above or below a threshold, for some minutes
nfr: Very high write rate — the main challenge
Graphs load in about a second
Keep a year of history cheaply
cap: Batch on the agent; Kafka in front of storage
Store by series and time, read contiguous blocks
model: All points of one series sit together
A graph reads a few contiguous blocks
Small table, cached by the engine

options.name: Server pulls (scrapes)
pros: Easy to see a host is down
cons: Hard at hundreds of thousands of hosts

trade.chosen: Push from agents to collectors in each data centre, with local buffering.
trade.flip: A small fleet where one server can scrape everything — then pull is simpler.

fail: Agents retry another collector and buffer on local disk
Missing data for 3 intervals raises a "host down" alert
Kafka holds the data; alerts read from the stream, not the DB
staff: Asks about **cardinality** first — one bad label (a user id) can create millions of series and kill the store.
Treats **missing data as a signal** — a dead host sends nothing, so "no data" must alert.
Plans **monitoring the monitor** — per data centre, so an outage never blinds you.
Talks cost: **downsampling and retention** tiers, with numbers.

steps: Telegraf or OpenTelemetry collector on every host
Scrapes local stats, adds labels (host, cluster, DC), batches 10 s of points, compresses, sends. Buffers to local disk if the gateway is down.
Agent-side batching is the biggest win for write volume.
Stateless HTTP/gRPC service per data centre behind a load balancer
Validates, rejects high-cardinality labels, produces to Kafka with key = series_id (hash of metric + labels).
Keying by series keeps one series in order on one partition.
Kafka topic metrics, ~hundreds of partitions, 24 h retention
Absorbs spikes and lets three independent consumers read: storage, rollups, alerting.
Decouples writers from slow storage; replay after a storage outage.
Time-series DB: M3, VictoriaMetrics, or Cassandra with (series_id, time_block) partitions
Writes points into 2-hour blocks per series with delta-of-delta timestamps and XOR-compressed values (Gorilla encoding), ~1.4 bytes per point.
A purpose-built TSDB beats a generic DB 10× on space and range-scan speed.
Flink job: keyBy(series) → 1-min and 1-hour tumbling windows → avg / max / min / count
Writes rollup series back to the TSDB; raw data expires after 14 days.
Long-range graphs read rollups, not raw points.
Alert evaluator (Flink job or Prometheus-style ruler) reading the stream
Keeps per-rule, per-series state: "value > 70% for 5 min" fires only after 5 minutes of consecutive breaches. A missing-data timer fires "no data" alerts.
Evaluating on the stream avoids polling the TSDB and keeps alerts fast.
Groups alerts by service, dedupes repeats, applies silences during maintenance.
Grouping prevents an incident from sending 500 pages.
Query service with a PromQL-like language; Grafana for dashboards
Chooses resolution from the range (raw < 2 days, 1-min < 90 days, else 1-hour), fans out to TSDB shards, merges.
Picking resolution by range keeps every graph fast.

write.title: host-1 reports memory = 72%
steps: The agent collects 2,000 stats, batches 10 s of points, compresses them.
The gateway validates labels and rejects high-cardinality ones.
It produces to Kafka with key = series_id, so one series stays ordered.
TSDB writers append the point into the series' current 2-hour block (Gorilla-compressed).
In parallel, Flink updates the 1-minute and 1-hour rollups.
And the alert evaluator updates "mem > 70% for 5 min" state for host-1.

read.title: "Graph memory for host-1..3 over the last week"
steps: Grafana sends the query with the time range and step.
The query service picks the 1-minute rollup (range is a week), finds the 3 series ids.
It range-scans those series' blocks on their shards in parallel.
Merges and downsamples to the step, returns ~30K points.

title: Key-value store on files
statement: Design a key-value store on top of a minimal file API: you can create a file, append bytes to it, and read bytes from an offset. Keys fit in memory; values do not and must be read from disk.

variants.text: Key-value store on a file interface: append, read bytes at an offset, create.
Design a Key-Value Store — components, data partitioning, replication, consistency model, use cases.
Design KV store — started with purpose, storage, compute, sharding.
variants.note: Did not follow a standard structure.

variants.text: Key-value based system — internal architecture, append-only log file management, log compaction, disk cleanup strategies.

guide.gist: Build a key-value store on top of a **simple file API** (create, append, read bytes at an offset). Keys fit in memory, values do not. This is the **Bitcask** design: append values to a log file, keep an **in-memory index key → (file, offset, size)**.
clarify: Exact interface given?
Yes — append, read at offset, create. So no in-place updates — everything is append.
Delete support?
Needs tombstones and compaction.
Durability on crash?
Need to rebuild the index from files.
Single machine or distributed?
Start with one node; distribution is a follow-up.
numbers: Keys fit in memory: say 100M keys × 50 bytes ≈ 5 GB of index — OK.
Values on disk, maybe TBs.
A read = one in-memory lookup + one disk read.
parts: All writes append (key, value, length, checksum) here.
Hash map key → (fileId, offset, size). Updated after each append.
When the active file is big, close it and start a new one.
Background: copy only the latest value of each live key into new files, then drop old files.
Small file per data file listing key → offset, so restart is fast.
deep: Write path
Append to the end of the active file (fast, sequential), then update the index. An update is just a new append — the index points to the newest one.
Read path
Look up the key in memory, then read exactly `size` bytes at `offset`. One disk read.
Delete and compaction
Append a tombstone; index removes the key. Compaction later removes old values and tombstones to free space.
Crash recovery
Rebuild the index by scanning files (or hint files). A checksum per record detects a half-written last record — ignore it.
The distributed version (two of the three LeetCode reports)

Partition keys with **consistent hashing** (virtual nodes so adding a node moves little data). Replicate each partition to 3 nodes. Consistency: quorum reads/writes (W + R > N) for strong-ish reads, or leader-per-partition for simple strong consistency. Name the trade: availability during partitions vs fresh reads.
followups: Range queries (all keys between A and B)?
A hash index cannot do it — use a sorted structure (LSM tree / SSTables) instead. Say the trade-off.
Keys no longer fit in memory.
Move to an LSM tree: sorted files with a sparse index and Bloom filters.
Make it distributed.
Partition keys by consistent hashing; replicate each partition to 3 nodes.
Concurrent writers?
One writer thread appends (serialises writes); readers read in parallel.
Partitioning, replication and consistency — how?

Consistent hashing with virtual nodes; replication factor 3; leader-follower per partition (simple, strong) or leaderless quorum N=3, W=2, R=2 (more available). Hinted handoff and read repair for leaderless.
Disk cleanup — when do you run compaction, and does it hurt reads?
Compact when dead data in a file passes a threshold (e.g. 50%); run in the background with an I/O budget; readers keep using old files until the swap is atomic.
How do you know what is safe to delete after compaction?
Write the new file fully, fsync, update the index to point at it, then delete the old file. A crash in between leaves extra files, never lost data.
mistakes: Trying to update values in place — the API only appends.
Forgetting compaction — disk grows forever.
No checksum for torn writes after a crash.
guide.say: "Append-only data files, an in-memory index of key to file and offset, background compaction, and hint files for fast restart — the Bitcask design."

fr: Values bigger than memory, kept on disk
nfr: No data loss when a node dies
rows: all writes go to the end
cap: Keys fit in memory — a hash index works
Values stay on disk, one read per get
Spread over nodes with consistent hashing
model: Writes always go to the end of the active file

options.name: Leaderless quorum (N=3, W=2, R=2)
pros: Stays available when a node dies
cons: Conflicts to resolve; more complex reads

trade.chosen: Leader per partition with two followers — strong and simple.
trade.flip: If writes must never pause, even for seconds, go leaderless with quorums.

fail: A short pause on its partitions
A follower becomes leader; index rebuilt from hint files on restart
Each record has a checksum — a half-written last record is ignored
Compaction rewrites live keys into new files and deletes old ones
staff: States the **consistency choice** and what it costs, instead of "it is consistent".
Knows the **storage engine**: append-only log, index, compaction — and when an LSM tree is better.
Explains **crash safety step by step**: checksum, write new file, fsync, swap, then delete.
Plans **adding a node** with little data movement (virtual nodes).

steps: Client library with a cached partition map; consistent hashing with virtual nodes
hash(key) → partition → leader node. The map is refreshed from the metadata store when a node replies "not mine".
No extra hop through a proxy. Virtual nodes make adding a node move little data.
Stores which node leads which partition and the in-sync followers; runs leader election when a node dies.
Here a coordination service IS justified: exactly one leader per partition.
Append (key, value_len, value, CRC32) to the active data file; fsync per batch
Then update the in-memory hash map key → (file_id, offset, size). Acknowledge after the followers have the record (sync replication).
Sequential appends are the fastest disk write; batching fsyncs keeps throughput high.
Hash map lookup, then pread(file, offset, size)
Exactly one disk read per get; the OS page cache makes hot values free.
Keys fit in memory, values do not — the Bitcask trade.
Leader ships each appended record to 2 followers; quorum or all-sync ack
On leader death, the metadata store promotes the most up-to-date follower.
Leader-per-partition = simple strong consistency. Alternative: leaderless quorum (Dynamo) for higher write availability.
Tombstone records; background compaction thread with an I/O budget
Compaction copies only the latest value of live keys into new files, writes a hint file, swaps the index atomically, deletes old files.
Hint files (key → offset) per data file
On restart, load hint files instead of scanning all data; a bad CRC on the last record means it was torn — ignore it.
Restart in seconds instead of minutes.

write.title: put("user:42", profile)
steps: The client hashes the key and finds the partition leader from its cached map.
It appends (key, length, value, CRC) to the active data file; fsync per batch.
It updates the index: user:42 → (file 7, offset 9,812, size 1,024).
It replicates the record to 2 followers and acknowledges after they have it.

read.title: get("user:42")
steps: Hash the key → partition → leader (or a follower if slightly stale reads are fine).
One in-memory lookup gives (file 7, offset 9,812, size 1,024).
One pread of 1,024 bytes at that offset (often served by the page cache).

title: Top-N in the last 24 hours
statement: A service runs on several hundred machines. Design a way to answer "which N items were requested most in the previous 24 hours" (a fixed day, not an arbitrary window) — for example the most searched strings of a search service, or the most requested keys of a distributed key-value store.

variants.text: Top-N most requested items in the last 24 hours across several hundred machines.
Top K heavy hitters over time windows of 5 minutes, 1 hour and 24 hours.
variants.note: Interviewer satisfied, but the candidate added a coordination service that was not needed and it caused a disagreement.

variants.text: Trending articles / Top-K videos — 2 LeetCode Discuss reports (lesson 11.2).

guide.gist: Find the **top N most frequent items over a fixed 24-hour window** across hundreds of machines. You cannot ship every request to one place, so each machine **counts locally**, and you **merge** counts. Exact vs approximate is the key trade-off.
clarify: Exact top N, or approximately right is fine?
Exact needs much more memory and network. Approximate allows Count-Min Sketch / Space-Saving.
"Last 24 hours (not any 24 hours)" — a fixed day or a sliding window?
The wording says a specific window — fixed hourly buckets make this easy.
How big is N? 10 or 10,000?
Small N → small heaps.
How fast must the answer be? Ad hoc query or a daily report?
Decides precompute vs on-demand merge.
numbers: 500 machines × 10K req/s = 5M req/s.
Distinct keys could be millions per hour — cannot send all counts every second.
Per machine per hour: keep top 10K with counts → 500 × 10K = 5M entries to merge per hour. Fine.
parts: Counts keys per hour (hash map, or Space-Saving / Count-Min Sketch to cap memory).
Each hour, send the local top-K (K bigger than N, e.g. 10× N) with counts to an aggregator.
Merges counts per hour bucket across machines.
The answer for "last 24 hours" = merge of 24 hour buckets → top N.
deep: Why local top-K is approximate
An item that is #10,001 on every machine can still be #1 overall. Fix: send more than N (10× N) and add a second pass for exact counts of the candidates, or accept small error and say so.
Count-Min Sketch + heap
Fixed memory counts with small overestimate; a heap keeps current top-K. Good when keys are too many to store exactly.
Sliding vs fixed
Hourly buckets give a window accurate to one hour. Need minute accuracy → minute buckets (1,440 of them).
Several windows at once (5 min, 1 hour, 24 hours)
Keep minute buckets. 5 min = merge 5 buckets; 1 hour = 60; 24 hours = merge hourly rollups (each hour merged once and stored). Same pipeline, three cheap merges.
followups: Exact answer is required.
Two passes: first collect candidate keys from every machine's top-K, then ask every machine for exact counts of those candidates.
Query must return in milliseconds.
Keep a precomputed rolling result updated every hour (or minute).
One machine is down for an hour.
Its bucket is missing — mark the result as partial, backfill when it returns (agents buffer locally).
Different windows: last 1 hour, last 7 days.
Same hourly buckets — merge 1 or 168 of them.
Do you need a coordination service (ZooKeeper)?

No — a candidate lost points adding one. Machines just send counts to aggregators partitioned by key; nothing here needs leader election or locks. Only add a component when you can say exactly what breaks without it.
mistakes: Sending every request to a central counter.
Merging only top-N from each machine and calling it exact.
Not asking exact vs approximate.
guide.say: "Count locally in hourly buckets, ship each machine's top-K, merge 24 buckets for the answer — approximate by default, with a second exact pass if needed."

fr: Count requests per item across all machines
Top K for 5 minutes, 1 hour and 24 hours
nfr: Small error is usually fine — confirm
cap: Never send every request to one place
Each machine sends its top 10× K
model: Each key is counted on one aggregator
Long windows merge 24 rollups, not 1,440 buckets

options.name: Approximate (Count-Min Sketch + heap)
cons: Small overcount; rare items can be wrong

trade.chosen: Approximate, and say the error bound — confirm with the interviewer first.
trade.flip: If it is used for billing or rewards, it must be exact: do a second exact pass on the candidates.

fail: Partition moves to another aggregator; machines resend
One machine is slow to report
Mark the minute as partial; backfill when data arrives
Local pre-aggregation means one key is one number, not millions of messages
staff: Asks **exact or approximate** before designing — it changes everything.
Uses **one pipeline for all windows** (minute buckets, hour rollups) instead of three systems.
**Adds nothing that is not needed** — a candidate lost points for an unneeded coordination service.
States the **error bound** and when a second exact pass is required.

steps: In-process hash map (or Count-Min Sketch + min-heap) inside each app server
Every request does map[item]++. Every 10 s the server sends its counts — only the items it saw, or its local top 10×K — and resets.
Turns millions of events into thousands of messages. Without it, Kafka carries one message per request.
Kafka topic local-counts, partitioned by hash(item)
Each message is (item, count, server, time). Same item → same partition → same Flink worker.
Partitioning by item means one worker owns all counts of an item — no cross-worker merge.
Flink job: keyBy(item) → 1-minute tumbling event-time window → sum
Flink keeps per-item counts in keyed state (RocksDB). Watermarks close a window when late data is unlikely; allowed lateness ~30 s.
Flink gives windows, state, checkpoints and exactly-once with Kafka. Alternatives: Kafka Streams (simpler, in-app), Spark Structured Streaming (micro-batch).
Flink ProcessWindowFunction with a size-K min-heap per partition, then a global merge task
Each parallel task emits its local top-K for the minute; one downstream task merges them into the final minute top-K.
Two-level top-K keeps the final merge tiny.
Flink checkpoints to S3/HDFS every ~30 s; Kafka offsets stored in the checkpoint
If a worker dies, the job restarts from the last checkpoint and replays Kafka from the saved offsets — counts are neither lost nor doubled.
This is why a stateful stream processor beats hand-written consumers here.
Redis sorted sets: key topk:min:<minute>, ZINCRBY item count; TTL 25 h
5-minute answer = ZUNIONSTORE of the last 5 minute-sets, then ZREVRANGE 0 K-1.
Sorted sets give ranked reads in O(log n). Small and fast.
Hourly rollup job writes each hour's top 10×K to Cassandra/Pinot (key: hour)
24-hour answer = merge 24 hourly lists in the API. Never merge 1,440 minute sets per request.
Rollups keep long-window queries cheap. Exact counts, if required, come from a second pass over candidates.
Stateless service + a small result cache (refresh every 10 s)
Picks the source by window: Redis for ≤ 1 h, hourly store for 24 h. Returns items with counts.
No coordination service anywhere — nothing here needs leader election or locks.

write.title: A request for item "linkedin" is counted
steps: The app server does counts["linkedin"]++ in memory. No network call.
Every 10 s it sends (linkedin, 37, server-12, minute) to Kafka, keyed by item.
Flink adds 37 to linkedin's keyed state for this minute; at the window end it emits the minute's top-K.
The minute top-K list goes to the minute-topk topic.
A consumer does ZINCRBY topk:min:<minute> 37 linkedin (key expires in 25 h).
At the end of each hour the rollup job merges 60 minute lists.
…and stores that hour's top 10×K in the hour store.

read.title: "Top 10 for the last 5 minutes / 24 hours?"
steps: The dashboard asks the Query API for top 10, window = 5 min (or 24 h).
The API checks its 10-second result cache first.
5 min: ZUNIONSTORE of the last 5 minute-sets, then ZREVRANGE 0 9.
24 h: read 24 hourly lists from the hour store and merge them in the API.
Ranked items with counts are returned and cached for 10 s.

title: Typeahead for LinkedIn search
statement: Design autocomplete for LinkedIn's search bar: as the member types a few letters, suggest matching people, companies and more (for example "Ry" suggests a connection named Ryan). Follow-ups: scale the index to a billion members, and compute and return the top K results with low latency.

variants.text: Typeahead for the LinkedIn search bar, scaled to 1B users.
Typeahead / autosuggest — Exponent ×2, Glassdoor (lesson 2.2).

guide.gist: Suggestions while typing must come back in **under ~100 ms**. So you **precompute** the top suggestions for every prefix and serve them from memory. Personalisation (your connections first) and freshness (new names) are the follow-ups.
clarify: What do we suggest — people, companies, skills, all?
Different sources, mixed in one list.
Personalised (your network first) or the same for everyone?
LinkedIn: personalised matters a lot — "Ry" should show your connection Ryan.
How fresh? A new company must show within?
Minutes vs a day decides batch vs streaming updates.
Latency target?
Under 100 ms end to end, so the server part ~20–30 ms.
numbers: 1B members, many companies → ~1B+ entities.
Peak maybe 100K prefix queries/s (every keystroke).
Top-10 per prefix, prefixes up to ~10 chars → large but shardable by prefix.
parts: Trie or prefix → top-K list, built offline with popularity scores. In memory, sharded by prefix.
Your 1st/2nd-degree connections' names — small per member, fetched or cached at login.
Combines global and personal results, ranks (personal first), returns top 10.
Batch builds the global index daily; a streaming path adds new entities quickly.
Debounce (wait ~50 ms after typing), cancel old requests, cache recent prefixes.
deep: Precompute top-K per prefix
Ranking millions of matches at query time is too slow. Store the answer for each prefix ahead of time. Space grows, but memory is cheap compared to latency.
Personalisation without per-user tries
Global index for popular entities + a small per-user list of connections, merged at query time.
Freshness
Main index rebuilt daily; a small "recent additions" index updated in near real time and merged in.
followups: How to scale with 1 billion users in the index?
Shard the prefix index by prefix; replicate hot shards (short prefixes like "a" are hottest); cache top prefixes.
How to generate rank and return top K with low latency?
Scores computed offline (popularity, connections, recency), stored sorted per prefix, so query time is just a lookup + small merge.
Typos ("Rian" for "Ryan")?
Fuzzy matching with edit distance 1 on short candidate sets, or phonetic keys.
Privacy?
Only show names the viewer is allowed to see; filter blocked members.
mistakes: Ranking at query time over the whole dataset.
Forgetting personalisation for LinkedIn.
No client-side debounce/cancel.
guide.say: "Precompute top-K per prefix in a sharded in-memory index, merge with a small personal list of connections at query time, and keep it fresh with a small real-time index."

cap: In-memory lookups only, no ranking at query time
Shard by prefix, replicate hot short prefixes
Fetch at login, merge at query time
model: One lookup per keystroke; shard by prefix

trade.chosen: Precompute globally, and merge a small personal list at query time.
trade.flip: If the index were small (thousands of items), ranking at query time would be fine.

fail: A shard of the prefix index dies
Time-box it and return global results — never block typing
Keep serving the last good index; alert
staff: Moves work **offline**: precompute top-K per prefix, so query time is a lookup.
Designs for **personalisation without per-user indexes**: global index + small personal list.
Handles **hot short prefixes** ("a", "s") with replication and caching.
Sets a **latency budget** per hop, and degrades gracefully instead of blocking typing.

steps: Debounce ~50 ms, cancel stale requests, cache recent prefixes in the browser
Typing "ryan" sends maybe two requests, not four.
Cuts load 2–3× before any server is touched.
CDN or edge cache for anonymous / popular short prefixes, TTL ~minutes
Prefixes like "a", "li" are the hottest and identical for many users.
Absorbs the hottest traffic close to the user.
Daily Spark job over members, companies, schools
Scores each entity (popularity, profile quality), generates every prefix up to ~10 chars, keeps the top 20 per prefix, writes sorted shard files to S3.
All ranking work happens offline; query time is a lookup.
In-memory map prefix → top-K list, sharded by prefix range, 3 replicas
Nodes load the latest snapshot from S3 at deploy; a lookup is a hash-map read.
Microseconds per lookup; hot short-prefix shards get extra replicas.
Redis: member_id → connection names (1st and 2nd degree), loaded at session start
The service prefix-matches the small personal list and merges it above global results.
No per-user trie. Personal results first is what makes it feel like LinkedIn.
Kafka stream of new profiles / companies → small "recent" index updated in near real time
Merged into results until the next daily build absorbs them.
New company pages appear in minutes, not a day.
Calls prefix shard + personal + fresh in parallel with a 30 ms budget, merges, applies privacy filters, returns top 10.

title: Malicious IP denylist
statement: A small share of LinkedIn's traffic is malicious. Given a function that tells you whether a request is malicious, design a system that builds a list of bad IP addresses and keeps every one of LinkedIn's many web servers up to date with it.

variants.text: Denylist malicious IPs and keep every web server up to date (isMalicious given).
Design a distributed IP deny list: a function says whether an IP should be denied; build the denylist and sync it with all the servers.
In a system like LinkedIn, intercept malicious requests and deny them. Assume a service isMaliciousRequest is available.

guide.gist: Detect bad IPs in one place and push the list to thousands of web servers **quickly and reliably**. The real problem is **distribution**: every server must get updates fast, and the check on every request must cost almost nothing.
clarify: How fast must a new bad IP be blocked everywhere?
Seconds vs minutes changes push vs pull.
How big is the list? IPv4 only or IPv6 too?
A few million IPs fit in memory on each server. IPv6 needs prefixes (ranges), not single IPs.
Do entries expire?
Yes usually — IPs get reused. Add a TTL so the list does not grow forever.
Is a false positive (blocking a good user) worse than missing a bad one?
Decides how strict detection is and whether we need an appeal / allow-list path.
numbers: Say 10,000 web servers, 1M requests/s total.

Keeps the list in memory. Loads a snapshot at start, then applies deltas from the stream.

deep: Push vs pull

Pull every 30 s is simple but slow and makes 10,000 servers hit the service at once. Push through Kafka is fast (seconds). Best: **push deltas, plus a periodic pull of the version** to catch anything missed.
Never stale without knowing it
Each server knows its list version. If it falls too far behind (version gap or no update for N minutes) it reloads the snapshot and raises an alert.
What if the denylist service is down?
Web servers keep using their last list — fail open for availability, but the list is still mostly correct. Never block all traffic because the list could not load.
Ranges and IPv6
Store CIDR prefixes in a trie (longest-prefix match). One entry can block a whole bad subnet.
"Intercept malicious requests" (the second LeetCode wording)

Where you intercept matters: at the edge (load balancer / API gateway) so bad traffic never reaches services. The in-memory denylist check runs there. isMaliciousRequest is expensive, so call it asynchronously on a sample or on suspicious traffic and feed results into the denylist, rather than calling it on every request.
followups: A bad IP must be blocked in under 5 seconds everywhere.
Push via Kafka with servers subscribed directly; measure end-to-end lag as a metric and alert on it.
The list becomes 100M entries.
Use a Bloom filter in memory for the first check (no false negatives), and confirm hits against a local compact store. Or block by prefix instead of single IPs.
How do you unblock a wrongly blocked user?
Allow-list that overrides the denylist, an appeal path, and TTLs so mistakes expire on their own.
How do you check it is working?
Metrics: list version per server, lag, block rate, false-positive reports. Canary: add a test IP and confirm every server blocks it.
Must isMaliciousRequest run on every request?
Usually no — too slow. Check the cheap in-memory denylist on every request, run the expensive classifier async (or only on suspicious patterns), and add offenders to the list.
mistakes: Calling a remote service on every request — adds latency and a single point of failure.
Sending the full list every time instead of deltas.
No versioning — you cannot tell which servers are stale.
Running isMalicious inline and slowing every request.

statement: Design a distributed message queue.

guide.gist: Design a **Kafka-like** queue: producers append messages, consumers read them, messages are **durable** and **ordered within a partition**. LinkedIn built Kafka, so expect deep questions on partitions, replication and delivery guarantees.
clarify: Queue (each message to one consumer) or pub/sub (to many groups)?
Kafka style log does both via consumer groups.
Ordering needed?
Usually per key — so partition by key.
Delivery: at-least-once or exactly-once?
At-least-once + idempotent consumers is the common answer.
Retention — delete after read, or keep for days?
Log style keeps for days, so consumers can replay.
numbers: Say 1M messages/s × 1 KB = 1 GB/s in.
Replication factor 3 → 3 GB/s disk writes across the cluster.

api: consume(topic, group) → messages from an offset
parts: A topic is split into partitions; each partition is an append-only log on disk.

Each partition is read by one consumer in a group; the group stores its offset.

deep: Why an append-only log is fast
Sequential disk writes and reads, OS page cache, batching, zero-copy send. That is why Kafka handles huge throughput.
Replication and acks
Leader writes, followers copy. With acks=all, a message is acknowledged only when all in-sync replicas have it — no loss if the leader dies.
Delivery guarantees
Consumer processes then commits the offset → at-least-once (may repeat after a crash). Make consumers idempotent. Exactly-once needs transactions — say it is costly.
followups: A consumer is slow (lag grows).
Add consumers up to the number of partitions; more partitions for the future; alert on lag.
A broker dies.
Controller elects a new leader from in-sync replicas; producers and consumers refresh metadata.
Ordering across the whole topic?
Only with one partition — kills throughput. Per-key ordering is the usual answer.
Delayed / scheduled messages?
Separate delay topics or a timer service — Kafka does not do it natively.
mistakes: A single queue with no partitions.
Promising global ordering and high throughput together.
Deleting messages on read (no replay).

Each partition is read by one consumer in the group; the consumer commits its offset after processing.

title: Distributed job scheduler (fetch machines, execute, alert)
statement: Design a distributed job scheduler. You are given an API to fetch machines for running jobs. Design a system that schedules jobs, executes them, and triggers alerts.

variants.text: Design a distributed job scheduler. You are given an API to fetch machines for running jobs. Design a system that schedules jobs, executes them, and triggers alerts.

guide.gist: Run jobs at the right time on machines you **ask for through an API**, make sure each job runs **once**, survive scheduler crashes, and **alert** on failures. The core: a durable job store, a way to find **due jobs** quickly, **leases** so two schedulers never run the same job, and a clear **job state machine**.
clarify: One-off jobs, recurring (cron), or both? Dependencies between jobs?
Recurring needs a "next run time"; dependencies need a DAG — say if out of scope.
Exactly once, or at least once with idempotent jobs?
Exactly once is very hard; at-least-once + idempotent jobs is the usual answer.
What does the machine API give us — a free machine on request? Can machines die mid-job?
Decides retries and heartbeats.
How many jobs per day, and how late is acceptable?
Decides how we find due jobs (DB index vs time buckets).
Alert on what — failure, timeout, too many retries, late start?
Defines the alerting rules.
numbers: Say 10M job runs/day ≈ 120/s average, peaks of 2K/s at the top of the hour (cron jobs bunch up).

deep: No double runs

A scheduler **claims** a run with an atomic update: `SET state=claimed, lease_until=now+30s WHERE id=? AND state=due`. Only one wins. If it crashes, the lease expires and another scheduler picks it up.
State machine
scheduled → claimed → running → succeeded / failed → (retry → scheduled) / dead. Every change is an atomic update with the expected old state, so late messages cannot move a run backwards.
Machine failure mid-job

Workers heartbeat every few seconds. Missed heartbeats → the monitor marks the run lost and schedules a retry (with backoff), on a new machine from the API. Jobs must be idempotent because a retry may repeat work.
Top-of-hour spike
Partition due runs by hash across scheduler nodes; add small random jitter for jobs that do not need the exact second.
followups: Do you need ZooKeeper / a coordination service?

No heartbeats — a dead machine leaves a job "running" forever.
Scanning the whole job table every second.
Promising exactly-once.

title: Flexible in-memory cache — pluggable eviction, then distributed
statement:
Design a flexible in-memory cache with customizable capacity and eviction policies.

The cache should allow users to define:

Capacity: Specify how much data the cache can hold based on memory resources and data size.
Eviction Policy: Choose strategies for removing items when the cache is full, such as Least Recently Used (LRU) or Lowest Priority.
This flexibility ensures the cache can be tailored to meet specific requirements, balancing resource usage and performance.

(Reported follow-on: once the low-level design was agreed, extend it to many nodes in a distributed setup — the challenges, hot keys in a write-heavy setup, and some Redis internals.)

variants.text: Flexible in-memory cache with customisable capacity and eviction policies (LRU, lowest priority); LLD first, then HLD across many nodes — hot keys in a write-heavy setup, Redis internals.
variants.note: Round opened with project and leadership questions; HLD extension after the LLD was agreed.

guide.gist: Starts as **low-level design**: a cache whose **capacity** and **eviction policy** are configurable — so eviction must be a **plug-in (strategy pattern)**, not hard-coded LRU. Then it becomes **high-level design**: many nodes, sharding, replication, and **hot keys** in a write-heavy setup, with some Redis internals.
clarify: Capacity by number of items or by bytes?
"Based on memory and data size" → track bytes, so each entry needs its size.
Which policies must exist on day one? Can users add their own?
LRU and lowest-priority now; an interface so more can be added.
TTL as well?
Usually yes — expiry is separate from eviction.
Thread-safe?
Yes for a real cache — decide the lock design.
For the distributed part: read-heavy or write-heavy? Consistency needs?
The report says write-heavy with hot keys.
numbers: One node: say 32 GB, entries ~1 KB → ~30M entries; per-entry overhead (pointers, policy data) ~50–100 bytes.
Distributed: 1M ops/s across 20 nodes → 50K ops/s each — fine for in-memory.
One hot key at 200K writes/s overloads a single node — this is the hot-key problem.
api: Get(key) / Put(key, value, size, priority?, ttl?) / Remove(key)
parts: Dictionary key → entry (value, size, metadata). Tracks used bytes. Calls the policy on every event.
OnInsert / OnAccess / OnRemove / PickVictim. The core never knows which policy it has.
Doubly linked list in recency order — O(1) for every call.
Min-heap or SortedSet by (priority, insert order); ties → oldest.
Consistent hashing to place keys on nodes; replicas for availability; client library or proxy routes requests.
deep: Why a policy interface

The question's key word is "customisable". With a strategy interface, adding LFU or TTL-first eviction is a new class, not a change to the cache. Evict in a loop until `used + newSize <= capacity` — one big item may need several evictions.
Thread safety
Simple: one lock around each operation (a Get also changes LRU order, so it writes). Faster: shard the cache into N segments, each with its own lock and policy — approximate global LRU.
Hot keys, write-heavy
Spread one hot key: split it into sub-keys (key#1..key#N) and combine on read, or batch writes locally and flush. For reads: replicate the hot key or keep a small local cache on clients.
Redis internals they may ask
Single-threaded command execution (no locks, one core per instance), approximate LRU by sampling a few keys, persistence by RDB snapshots and AOF log, cluster mode with 16,384 hash slots.
followups: Add an LFU policy.
New class implementing the interface: frequency buckets with a min-frequency pointer, O(1). No change to the cache core.
An item bigger than the whole capacity?
Reject it (or do not cache it) — say it explicitly.
A node dies.
Consistent hashing moves only its keys; replicas serve them; the cache refills from the source. Expect a miss spike — protect the database (request coalescing).
Cache and database disagree.
Cache-aside with invalidation on write, short TTLs, and versioned keys for important data.
Why is Redis fast despite one thread?
In-memory, no locks, efficient data structures, I/O multiplexing; scale out with more instances.
mistakes: Hard-coding LRU inside the cache when the question says "customisable".
Counting items when capacity is in bytes.
Forgetting a Get changes LRU order (so it needs the lock).
Ignoring the hot-key problem in the distributed part.
guide.say: "A cache core that tracks bytes and delegates every eviction decision to a pluggable policy; then consistent hashing, replicas, and key splitting or local batching for hot keys."

statement: Design the collaborative coding tool LinkedIn uses for interviews. The candidate writes code and the interviewer watches it change live (assume only the candidate edits). There is also a drawing canvas that both people see in real time. The interviewer can invite more people to a pad by email. Finally, any interview can be replayed later, showing what happened at each moment.

Question says interviewer only watches. One writer makes sync much simpler — no merge conflicts.
How long is an interview, and how long do we keep replays?
Decides storage size and when to move old pads to cold storage.

Yes means we must store every change with a timestamp, not just snapshots.

numbers: Say 100K interviews a day, 1 hour each, ~3 people per pad.
Typing: ~5 events per second per active editor → 100K × 5 = 500K events/s at peak if all overlap; realistically ~50K events/s.
Each event ~50 bytes → 1 hour ≈ 18K events ≈ 1 MB per pad. 100K pads/day ≈ 100 GB/day. Cheap.

deep: Why an event log, not "save the file every few seconds"?

Saving the file loses the order of changes, so you cannot replay. With events you get three things from one store: live sync (broadcast the event), recovery (replay the log after a crash), and replay (play the log slowly). One source of truth.
Sync when only one person edits

The interviewee is the only writer, so the server just orders the events and forwards them. No conflict handling. If the interviewer is allowed to edit later, then we need OT (operational transform) or CRDT — mention this as the change point.
Drawing pad
Treat drawing the same way: each stroke is an event (points, colour, width). Batch the points every 50 ms so we do not send hundreds of tiny messages.
Replay as "video"
Do not record a real video. Store events and re-render them in the browser at the original timestamps. Much smaller, and you can jump to any point using the nearest snapshot.
followups: What if the WebSocket node crashes?
Clients reconnect to another node, tell it their last seq number, and get the missing events from the log. Nothing is lost because the event is written to the log before it is broadcast.
How do you make replay seek fast?
Snapshots every ~500 events. To jump to minute 40, load the nearest snapshot before it and apply only the events after it.
Now the interviewer can also edit. What changes?

Two writers can edit the same place at the same time. Use OT or a CRDT so both changes merge the same way on every screen. The event log stays — it now stores operations that the merge logic understands.
How do you secure the invite link?
Random unguessable pad id plus a signed token with expiry. Only invited emails can join; every join is logged.
Scale to 1 million live pads?
Shard pads across session nodes by padId (consistent hashing). Each node holds its pads in memory. The gateway routes by padId.

Forgetting late joiners: they need snapshot + events, not the full log from the start.

Jumping to CRDTs when the question says only one writer.

title: Service-to-service permissions
statement: A company runs many services that call each other. Design a permission system that decides which services may call which.

variants.text: In your InterviewDB list.

guide.gist: Decide **which service may call which** — service-to-service **authorization**. Two parts: **identity** (who is calling — mTLS certificates) and **policy** (is this caller allowed this API). The check must be **fast and local** on every call, so policies are pushed to each service.
clarify: Per service, or per API method too?
Finer policies (service A may call only GET /profile) mean bigger policy sets.
How many services and calls?
Thousands of services, millions of calls/s → no central check per call.
How fast must a policy change apply?
Seconds to minutes → push model.
Audit needed?
Yes usually — who called what, allowed or denied.
numbers: Say 3,000 services, 5M internal calls/s.
Policy rules maybe 100K — a few MB, fits in memory in each sidecar.
A central check per call would add a network hop to 5M calls/s — not acceptable.
api: Policy admin: POST /policies {caller, callee, method, allow}
parts: Each service gets a certificate (mTLS, SPIFFE-like id) from an internal CA; rotated automatically.
Source of truth for rules, versioned, with review/approval.
Pushes policy updates to every sidecar/library (like the denylist pattern).
Sidecar or library checks caller identity from mTLS + method against local policy.
Decisions sent async to a log pipeline.
deep: Authenticate, then authorize
mTLS proves the caller is service A (cannot be faked by a header). Then policy says if A may call this method.
Local decisions
Policies cached in memory at the callee — microsecond checks, and no dependency on a central service per call.
Default deny + rollout
New services start with no access; changes go through review; a "log-only" mode lets you test a policy before enforcing it.
followups: The policy service is down.
Callees keep their last policy version — calls continue. Alert if versions get old.
User context too (service A calls B on behalf of a user)?
Pass a signed token with the user identity; B checks both service and user permission.
How do you migrate thousands of existing services?
Log-only mode first, learn the actual call graph, generate policies from it, then enforce service by service.
Revoke a compromised service fast.
Revoke its certificate and push a deny policy — both propagate in seconds.

Trusting a "caller name" header without mTLS.
Enforcing new policies without a log-only test phase.
